passages.happening:
Moses speaks of the crossing that is about to happen. Israel will face nations ‘greater and stronger than you’, with cities fortified to the sky, and the tall Anakim, of whom people said, ‘Who can stand up to the sons of Anak?’ (verses 1-2). But God himself will go ahead, ‘as a consuming fire’ (verse 3).

Then Moses warns against a thought. When it is done, ‘do not say in your heart, “Because of my righteousness the LORD has brought me in to possess this land”’ (verse 4).

He says it three times over. “It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land, but it is because of their wickedness that the LORD your God is driving out these nations before you, to keep the promise He swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (verse 5).

“Understand, then, that it is not because of your righteousness that the LORD your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff-necked people” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 8 warned against one proud thought after success, that Israel's own strength did it. Chapter 9 warns against another, which is more dangerous because it sounds religious: that Israel's own goodness earned it.

A winning people naturally thinks that its victory proves its virtue. Moses cuts that off before the first battle. He gives two reasons for what is about to happen, and neither one is Israel. The first is the wickedness of the nations of the land. The second is the promise God swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

‘Righteousness’ in Hebrew means rightness in a relationship: living as one's duties to God and neighbor require. Three times in three verses Moses denies that Israel has it to show.

‘Stiff-necked’ is a farmer's picture. An ox that stiffens its neck will not bow to the yoke or turn when the driver calls. It names a stubborn refusal to be led. Moses uses it of his own people, to their faces, on the eve of their greatest gift.

A reader should be careful about what follows from this passage and what does not.

It does not say that Israel was better than the Canaanites. It says the reverse. The judgment on the nations is for wickedness, and Israel is told in the same breath that it has no goodness to boast of, and elsewhere that it will be judged in the same way if it does the same things (8:20).

It gives no people a reason for contempt toward another. The whole point of the passage is to take away the ground for feeling superior.

And it describes one people at one moment. It is not a way of explaining why any nation today prospers or suffers, and no nation may take it as a claim for itself.

The note on chapter 7, verses 1 to 5, sets out how Christians read the driving out of the nations.
passages.later:
God had told Abraham that his family would wait centuries for the land, ‘for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete’ (Genesis 15:16).

Paul begins a famous passage with the words of verse 4, ‘Do not say in your heart’ (Romans 10:6), and he writes of people who ‘sought to establish their own’ righteousness (Romans 10:3). He is writing as a Jew about a danger he knew from the inside, and he says the same of everyone: “Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin” (Romans 3:9).

Paul gives the Christian form of Moses' sentence: “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy” (Titus 3:5).

Jesus told of two men who went up to pray, one sure of his own goodness and one who could only say, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner’. It was the second who ‘went home justified’ (Luke 18:13-14).
passages.asks: Moses names a thought that is said ‘in your heart’. Ask whether, when things go well for you, some part of you concludes that you deserved it. And ask how you think about people whose lives have gone badly. The passage that forbids pride in one's own goodness also forbids looking down on anyone else.

passages.happening:
Moses now proves what he has just said. “Remember this, and never forget how you provoked the LORD your God in the wilderness. From the day you left the land of Egypt until you reached this place, you have been rebelling against the LORD” (verse 7).

He goes back to Horeb. He had gone up the mountain to receive the stone tablets of the covenant, and stayed forty days and nights without bread or water (verse 9). God gave him the tablets, ‘inscribed by the finger of God’ (verse 10).

Then God told him to go down at once, because the people had made a metal image (verse 12). God said, “Leave Me alone, so that I may destroy them and blot out their name from under heaven. Then I will make you into a nation mightier and greater than they are” (verse 14).

Moses came down with the tablets in his hands and saw the calf. “So I took the two tablets and threw them out of my hands, shattering them before your eyes” (verse 17).

He lay before God for another forty days and nights, without food or water, afraid of God's anger. “But the LORD listened to me this time as well” (verse 19). He prayed for Aaron too (verse 20). He burned the calf, ground it to dust, and threw the dust into the stream that ran down the mountain (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The fuller story is in Exodus 32 to 34. Moses retells it here with one aim, to show Israel what it is.

The timing is the terrible part. While God was writing ‘You shall have no other gods’ on stone at the top of the mountain, the people were casting an image at the bottom. Verse 12 says, ‘How quickly they have turned aside’. It was within weeks of hearing God's own voice.

The calf, a young bull, was a common religious sign in that world. In Canaan the bull was linked with the gods El and Baal. In Egypt a sacred bull was worshiped at Memphis. Many scholars think the calf was not meant as a new god. It may have been meant as a stand or a sign for Israel's own God, since Aaron announced a feast ‘to the LORD’ (Exodus 32:5). Either way it broke the command to make no image. Moses calls it ‘that sinful thing’.

Breaking the tablets was more than temper. In the ancient world, to smash a treaty tablet showed that the agreement was broken. Moses did it ‘before your eyes’. The covenant had been broken by the people before the stone was.

What he did to the calf, burning, crushing, grinding and scattering, was a known way of describing complete destruction. Nothing was left that could be picked up and honored.

God's words to Moses in verse 14 are a real offer. Moses could have become the father of a new and better nation. He turned it down. He went down the mountain and then lay on his face for forty days for the people who had done this.

Aaron is not spared in the telling. Israel's first high priest made the calf, and he lived only because his brother prayed.

These are hard words, and it matters who is speaking them. This is Israel's own teacher, in Israel's own Scriptures, telling his people the truth about themselves so that they will live. It is not a charge for anyone else to pick up and use against the Jewish people. The Bible speaks as plainly of the failures of the church.
passages.later:
Exodus tells the breaking of the tablets: Moses ‘burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain’ (Exodus 32:19).

Israel sang about this day in its own worship: “At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image” (Psalm 106:19). The same psalm remembers who stood in the gap: ‘had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach’ (Psalm 106:23).

Centuries later King Jeroboam set up two golden calves in the northern kingdom and said, “Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28). The books of Kings treat that as the root sin of the north.
passages.asks: The people made the calf while God was still speaking on the mountain. Ask how quickly you have turned, after a time when God was plainly near. And notice what Moses did with an offer to be made great at his people's cost. Ask whether there is anyone you are tempted to write off whom you are meant to pray for.

passages.happening:
The calf was not the only time. Moses lists others: Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah, and then Kadesh-barnea, where ‘you neither believed Him nor obeyed Him’ (verses 22-23). He sums up: “You have been rebelling against the LORD since the day I came to know you” (verse 24).

Then he tells them what he prayed during the forty days. “O Lord GOD, do not destroy Your people, Your inheritance, whom You redeemed through Your greatness and brought out of Egypt with a mighty hand. Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Overlook the stubbornness of this people and the wickedness of their sin” (verses 26-27).

He gave God a further reason. If Israel died in the desert, Egypt would say that the LORD ‘was not able to bring them into the land He had promised them’, or that he hated them (verse 28). “But they are Your people, Your inheritance, whom You brought out by Your great power and outstretched arm” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The names in verse 22 are places of earlier failure. At Taberah the people complained and fire broke out at the edge of the camp. At Massah they demanded water and tested God. At Kibroth-hattaavah they craved the food of Egypt. The stories are in Exodus 17 and Numbers 11. Kadesh was the refusal to enter the land.

The accusation ‘you have been rebelling’ stands at the start of this retelling, in verse 7, and at its end, in verse 24. Everything between is evidence.

Then look at the prayer. Moses has just spent a chapter saying how guilty Israel is, and he does not take a word of it back when he prays. He does not tell God that the people are sorry, or that they are not so bad. He admits ‘the stubbornness of this people and the wickedness of their sin’.

He rests his whole plea on God. He appeals to three things. The first is what God has already done: these are the people he redeemed. The second is what God has promised: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The third is God's name among the nations: what Egypt will say.

In verse 12 God had called Israel ‘your people, whom you brought out of Egypt’, speaking to Moses. Moses gives the words back. They are ‘Your people’, ‘whom You brought out’. He will not accept that they are his.

The prayer has no ending in this chapter. Its answer comes in chapter 10, where God tells Moses to cut two new tablets.
passages.later:
Exodus records that the prayer was heard: “So the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people” (Exodus 32:14).

Exodus also records how far Moses was willing to go: “But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written” (Exodus 32:32).

The New Testament says that the church has one who does always what Moses did for forty days: “Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Moses standing between a guilty people and their judgment is a pattern of that. The New Testament draws the line; this chapter makes no prediction.
passages.hard:
God said, ‘Leave Me alone, so that I may destroy them’, and then he listened to Moses. Did Moses' prayer change God's mind?

Christians who confess that God knows all things and does not change have read this in several ways.

One view holds that the threat was real and also conditional. It was the kind of warning the prophets gave, which could be turned aside by repentance or by prayer. God says through Jeremiah, “But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring” (Jeremiah 18:8). On this view God's character did not change. His response to the situation did.

Another view hears God's words as an invitation. By saying ‘Leave Me alone’ to the one man who could plead, God opened the door for him to plead. On this view the whole scene shows that God had chosen to act through his servant's prayer.

A third view, held by some modern theologians, is that God truly responds to prayer in ways that are not fixed beforehand.

These notes take no side. All agree on what the text wants a reader to see. Prayer is to be taken seriously. Moses prayed, and the people lived. The chapter does not explain how. It shows a God who binds himself to his promises and who listens when someone pleads for others.
passages.asks: Moses prayed for people who had wronged God and worn him out, and he based his prayer on God's promises and not on their merit. Ask who you could pray for in that way. And when you pray for yourself after a failure, ask what you are resting on: your regret, your record, or the mercy of God.
